history.heading: The Old Swiss Confederacy
paragraphs: The territory of Switzerland was home to the Celtic Helvetii, who were conquered by Rome, and later to Alemanni and Burgundians. In 1291, according to tradition, the three Alpine cantons of Uri, Schwyz and Unterwalden swore an oath of alliance, the founding of the Swiss Confederation, commemorated on 1 August. The legend of William Tell symbolises this struggle for freedom against the Habsburgs.

The Confederacy expanded and won victories against the Habsburgs and Burgundy. Swiss mercenaries were famous across Europe, and the Swiss Guard still protects the Pope. The Reformation, led by Zwingli in Zurich and Calvin in Geneva, divided the cantons. Swiss independence from the Holy Roman Empire was recognised in 1648.

history.heading: Modern Switzerland
paragraphs: Napoleon invaded in 1798 and created the Helvetic Republic. The 1815 Congress of Vienna recognised Swiss neutrality. After a brief civil war (the Sonderbund War) in 1847, Switzerland adopted a federal constitution in 1848, creating the modern state.

Switzerland stayed neutral in both world wars, though its policies toward refugees and Nazi gold have been criticised. The Red Cross was founded in Geneva in 1863. Women gained the vote at the federal level only in 1971. Switzerland joined the UN in 2002.

culture.heading: Four languages
paragraphs: Switzerland has four national languages: German (spoken by about 60 percent, mostly in Swiss German dialects), French, Italian and Romansh. Christianity is divided between Catholics and Protestants, and a growing share is non-religious. About a quarter of the population are foreign nationals.

Swiss traditions include yodelling, alphorns and Schwingen (Swiss wrestling). Food includes fondue, raclette, rösti and famous chocolate and cheeses such as Gruyère and Emmental. Skiing and hiking in the Alps are central to life, and Roger Federer is a national hero.

politics.heading: Direct democracy
paragraphs: Switzerland is a federal republic of 26 cantons with a unique system of direct democracy: citizens vote several times a year on national referendums and popular initiatives. The Federal Council, a seven-member executive drawn from the main parties, governs collectively; the presidency rotates annually.

Switzerland is neutral and not a member of the EU or NATO, but has close ties with the EU through bilateral agreements and is in Schengen. Geneva hosts many international organisations, including UN offices, the WHO and the Red Cross.

economy.heading: A wealthy economy
paragraphs: Switzerland is one of the world's wealthiest and most innovative countries. Key sectors include pharmaceuticals (Roche, Novartis), banking and wealth management (UBS, which took over Credit Suisse in 2023), insurance, precision machinery, watches (Rolex, Swatch), food (Nestlé) and commodity trading. Tourism is important.
The Swiss franc is a safe-haven currency. In 2025 the United States imposed high tariffs on Swiss goods, hurting exporters.
